analysis.one_liner: Authorizes one company to build the Keystone XL border pipeline without a presidential permit.
analysis.headline: Seventeen senators cosponsored the bill, but it never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written into law an authorization for TC Energy to build, connect, operate, and maintain the Keystone XL pipeline's border crossing in Phillips County, Montana, to bring Canadian oil into the United States. It also would have declared that no presidential permit was required, removing the executive branch's power to stop or condition the project. The bill was introduced two weeks after President Biden revoked the pipeline's permit, and it sat in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: TC Energy, the pipeline company named in the bill, gains a statutory right to build and operate the border segment without needing a presidential permit. Canadian oil sands producers gain a direct pipeline route to Gulf Coast refineries, lowering their transport costs. Construction and pipeline trades in Montana and along the route would have gained several thousand mostly temporary jobs during construction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: TC Energy and oil sands producers

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P., to construct, connect, operate, and maintain the pipeline facilities at the U.S.–Canada border in Phillips County, Montana, for importing oil from Canada.
Declares that no presidential permit under any executive order is required for the pipeline's construction or operation, taking the decision out of the executive branch's hands.
The bill builds on a presidential permit issued in March 2019, reviving the authorization that the executive branch had granted before it was revoked.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the long-term costs: the bill skips the cross-border permitting process, including environmental review and public comment, and the pipeline would carry oil from Canadian oil sands, whose extraction and transport carry higher climate and spill risks than most crude. Landowners along the route and taxpayers exposed to cleanup liability bear localized risks. The construction jobs are real but temporary; the pipeline's operation would employ few people permanently.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along the route and the public

drawbacks.text: The bill would waive the presidential permit process entirely — no environmental review, no public comment, no executive-branch veto — for one specifically named company.

By naming a single corporation in statute and exempting it from executive-order permitting, the bill sets a precedent of Congress overriding the standard cross-border review that applies to every other international pipeline.

Keystone XL would carry Canadian oil sands crude, which is more carbon-intensive to produce than most oil; an honest supporter concedes the climate cost even while valuing the construction jobs and energy supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill was jobs — several thousand temporary construction jobs — and energy supply from a friendly ally. But the bill's centerpiece was not a jobs program; it was a statutory carve-out for one named company from the presidential permitting process, which means skipping environmental review and public input on a cross-border pipeline. The jobs would have lasted a few years; the climate and spill-risk exposure would have lasted for the pipeline's life. And the debate was largely moot by the time the bill died: TC Energy had already cancelled the project.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines introduced the bill on February 2, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was ever listed — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — for the remainder of the Congress.
The authorization the bill would grant references a presidential permit issued March 29, 2019, showing the bill's purpose was to restore a permit the executive branch had granted and later revoked.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: TC Energy had already cancelled the Keystone XL project in June 2021, taking a multibillion-dollar write-off, so the bill's death changed little for the company. The winners were opponents of the pipeline, who kept the presidential permitting process — with its environmental review and public comment — intact for any future cross-border project.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline opponents; the project was already cancelled

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to statutorily authorize the Keystone XL border crossing in his home state and waive the presidential permit requirement.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democrat to do so.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in his committee for the entire Congress.

against.name: President Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Revoked the Keystone XL presidential permit on his first day in office, two weeks before this bill was introduced to override that decision.

against.name: Environmental and climate advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a years-long campaign against the pipeline on climate and tribal-land grounds, keeping the political cost of reviving it high.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 16 of 50 Republican senators backed the bill, and a single Democrat joined them; no vote was ever taken, but the underlying dispute over the permit split cleanly along party lines, with a Democratic president revoking the permit and a Democratic-run Senate never acting on the override.

industries.note: The bill names this one company and gives it a statutory right to build and run the border segment, permanently exempt from presidential permitting. Construction would have brought temporary jobs to Montana and route communities, but the exemption also removes the environmental review and public comment that apply to every other cross-border pipeline.

A direct pipeline to Gulf refineries would cut their transport costs and support expanded heavy-crude production, which carries higher carbon emissions borne by the public rather than by the producers.

industries.industry: U.S. Gulf Coast refineries configured for heavy crude
industries.note: These refineries would gain a reliable, cheaper heavy-crude feedstock from Canada, which can support lower fuel input costs — though cheaper feedstock does not reliably reach consumers at the pump.
